name: Yukpa
confidence_why: Largo 2011 and Hanes 1952, working independently on Colombian Yukpa, both describe lexically contrastive stress that falls by default on the penultimate syllable and differ only on whether long vowels attract it, while the second-syllable rhythmic pattern in Meira 2005 comes from a preliminary sketch of Venezuelan Yukpa that its author himself lists as an open question.

new_statements.quote: 1.3. Prosodic phonemes are stress /ˊ/ and length /·/. Stress is phonemic as seen in á·ko friend and a·kó brother. In general however, stress occurs on a long vowel: tó·makaçi work. If there is no long vowel in the word, stress usually occurs on the penultimate vowel: tá?špo dig. But note also minéš don't look!. In words containing more than one long vowel, the penultimate long vowel is usually stressed: ne·ká·ta he died. A second stress occurs in some words: sá·kusékyapa I'm going to eat. [...] Tone or intonation may prove to be phonemic, but at present there is insufficient data regarding this.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog lists Yukpa (catalog-all-2026-09-12) with an empty rule and there are no existing stress statements; Hanes supplies the placement rule (length-attracted stress, default penultimate, contrastive, with a second stress in some words) for the Colombian (Eroca/Iroka valley) dialect, so it fills the blank rather than agreeing or contradicting a recorded placement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is contrastive (minimal pair á·ko 'friend' / a·kó 'brother') but in general predictable from vowel length: stress falls on the long vowel; with more than one long vowel, on the penultimate long vowel; with no long vowel, usually on the penultimate vowel. Stress and length are the two prosodic phonemes; tone/pitch is possibly lexical on two word pairs but undetermined.
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'A second stress occurs in some words: sá·kusékyapa I'm going to eat' (p. 147) — a second (secondary) stress is noted but no rule is given.
new_statements.exceptions: Lexical minimal pair á·ko 'friend' vs a·kó 'brother' (stress phonemic); minéš 'don't look!' with final stress although it has no long vowel; all placement statements hedged with 'in general' / 'usually'. Two word pairs (kó·ko 'night'/'dry', yáçi 'opossum'/'leaf') may show lexical pitch; author says data insufficient and contrasts unverified in context (pp. 147-148).
new_statements.identity_note: Hanes 1952 fn. 1 (p. 146): 'This paper is based on the dialect of Motilone spoken in the Eroca Valley of the Andes mountains, located in the northeastern part of the Department of Magdalena, Colombia, S.A.', data gathered 1948-1950 from monolingual informants, checked with Eugene Nida. 'Motilone (Carib)' is the Cariban Yukpa/Yuko of the Serranía de Perijá (Iroka variety), not the Chibchan Barí who are also called Motilón; WALS and Glottolog assign the work to yukp1241 (ISO yup, WALS ykp), so it is about this language.

readall_conflicts: Within the assigned work there is no conflict. Across the folder there is one to flag: Meira 2005 (CILLA-II paper on Venezuelan Yukpa, already held by the project from the 2026-09-16 pass, lines 216-231) says the language lacks distinctive vowel length and nasality and describes a preliminary rhythmic (iambic) system: 'El acento primario cae normalmente en la segunda sílaba, pero hay casos de acento inicial, sobre todo en ciertas formas verbales' with the caveat 'interpretaciones preliminares, sin estudio acústico detallado'. Hanes 1952 instead treats length as phonemic and makes stress follow the long vowel (else penultimate), with lexical minimal pairs; for a disyllable Hanes' default is initial (tá?špo 'dig'), Meira's is second-syllable. The two describe different dialects (Hanes: Colombian Eroca/Iroka valley, 1948-50; Meira: Venezuelan Yukpa, 2005) and Meira's statement is explicitly preliminary, so this is a dialect/analysis difference rather than a refutation, but a catalog rule should carry the dialect label. Largo's orthography note (sec. 1.1.1) marks a tilde on nouns whose stress departs from the unmarked pattern (potá 'escarabajo' vs pota 'boca mía'; pó 'yuca' vs po 'en'), which is consistent with Hanes' claim that stress is contrastive against a default.

sources.quote: 'el único fenómeno suprasegmental de interés parece ser el acento. En la familia caribe hay diversos casos de acentos rítmicos (yámbicos)… En yukpa, parece existir un sistema rítmico semejante, pero casi sin alargamiento; la intensidad y el tono son aparentemente más importantes. El acento primario cae normalmente en la segunda sílaba, pero hay casos de acento inicial, sobre todo en ciertas formas verbales. (Los ejemplos abajo son interpretaciones preliminares, sin estudio acústico detallado.)' exx.: kekeke [ke.ˈke.ke], kasapana [ka.ˈsa.pa.na], kasenopano [ka.ˈse.no.ˌpa.no], éwapo [ˈe.wa.po],

tone.quote: En cuanto al acento se observa: sí la palabra tiene una sílaba pesada, el acento recae sobre esta sílaba, mientras que si la palabra está compuesta de sílabas livianas el acento recae sobre la primera sílaba como se evidencia en estos ejemplos: Shaatre (tucán), nono (tierra), kayi (alto), yaari (hoja).
tone.locator: p. 59, introductory section, paragraph beginning 'En mi análisis de las lenguas Caribes de noroccidente'
tone.translation: As for stress, one observes: if the word has a heavy syllable, the stress falls on that syllable, whereas if the word is made up of light syllables the stress falls on the first syllable, as shown in these examples: Shaatre (toucan), nono (earth), kayi (tall), yaari (leaf).

tone.quote: La pronunciación en Iroka se caracteriza por que las sílabas de una palabra son producidas como si fueran silabas con un acento independiente a manera de falsete muy diferente en Menkwe en el que la pronunciación es mas plana con respecto a los hablantes de Iroka.
tone.locator: p. 13, sec. 2.2.1 'Variantes de Iroka y Menkwe (OC-YC)', point 2
tone.translation: Pronunciation in Iroka is characterized by the syllables of a word being produced as if they were syllables with an independent accent, in a falsetto-like manner, very different from Menkwe, where pronunciation is flatter compared with Iroka speakers.
tone.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
